result:
The city kept its lost minutes in a basement beneath the public library.

This was not advertised. The library’s signs directed visitors to Fiction, Local History, and the restrooms. To find the basement, you had to ask the woman at the returns desk what time it was. If she told you the time, you were not ready. If she said, “Which time?” she would hand you a brass key.

I found out on a Tuesday after missing a train.

The train had pulled away while I stood on the platform reading a message from my mother. It said, *Call when you have a minute.* I had not called her in eleven months. I read the message twice, put my phone away, and looked up at the empty tracks.

At the library, the woman at the desk said, “Which time?” before I had asked anything.

Downstairs, the room was bright and crowded with filing cabinets. A man in a green cardigan sat behind a counter, polishing a teaspoon.

“I lost seven minutes,” I told him.

“People usually start with a story.”

“I missed a train.”

He set down the spoon. “You can look for them, if you like.”

He gave me a drawer number. Inside were hundreds of narrow envelopes, each labeled with a date and a location: a grocery queue, a stairwell, the kitchen of an apartment I had left years ago. I opened the envelope marked *Tuesday, station platform*. It held a strip of pale paper. On it was written: *Seven minutes spent imagining the phone call instead of making it.*

“That doesn’t seem lost,” I said.

The man looked up from his spoon. “No?”

I went back to the drawer. I had been late for work because I could not decide which shirt to wear. I had stood beside my father’s hospital bed, trying to remember the name of a bird outside the window. I had sat in my car after a party until the streetlights went off. Each envelope held a minute I could describe but had never quite occupied.

At the bottom was one labeled *Sunday, my mother’s house*. I knew the date. I had gone to tell her I was moving across the country. She was making soup, cutting carrots into coins. We spoke about boxes and rent and the weather there. I stayed for an hour, then left.

The envelope was heavy. I slid out the paper.

*Fourteen minutes available while the soup simmered. Neither person mentioned the move.*

“I want those back,” I said.

The man folded his hands. “What would you do with them?”

“I’d tell her why I was going.”

He waited.

“I’d ask her if she was angry.”

He waited a little longer, but I had no more words.

From somewhere among the cabinets came the ticking of many small clocks, each one a little out of step with the others. The man placed the teaspoon in a drawer.

“Can I have them?” I asked.

“You can take the envelope.”

I put it in my coat pocket. By then I had missed the next train, too.

Outside, rain had begun in the uncertain way it sometimes does, a few drops spaced so far apart they seemed unrelated. I walked to the station slowly. At a crossing, I took out my phone and called my mother.

She answered on the fourth ring. There were voices behind her and the clatter of dishes.

“Hello,” I said.

“Oh,” she said, with a pleased surprise she made no effort to hide. “Is everything all right?”

“Yes. I missed my train.”

“Where are you?”

“Still here.”

A bus went by, throwing water over the curb. I moved back under the awning of a closed shop. My mother asked when the next train was. I said I didn’t know. She told me she had bought a little lamp for the table by her bed. She had seen it in a window for weeks and gone in for it that morning.

“What color?” I asked.

“Yellow glass. It makes the room look warm even when it’s cold.”

We spoke until I reached the station. I told her about the rain. She told me the soup she was making had too much salt. When she asked if I remembered the old kitchen, I said yes, and told her about the day I left.

“I remember,” she said.

“I wanted to say more.”

“I thought you might.”

The announcement for my train sounded overhead. I could hear her washing something at the sink.

“Were you angry with me?” I asked.

“For moving? No.” She paused. “I was angry that you thought you had to give me good reasons. I knew you wanted to go.”

I had not known she knew. I stood against a pillar while people moved around me.

“I was afraid you’d ask me to stay,” I said.

“I nearly did.”

We heard the train arrive through the phone, brakes squealing on the rails. My mother said, “You’ll miss that one as well.”

“I might.”

“Get on it,” she said. “Call me when you’re home.”

I boarded just before the doors closed. From my pocket I took the envelope, softened now by the rain. The paper inside still described fourteen minutes in her kitchen. Nothing had been crossed out or corrected. I put it away and found a seat by the window.

We passed the library as the train left the station. Its upstairs windows were lit; from here, the basement was invisible. I could see the returns desk for a moment, and a woman leaning across it to speak to the librarian. Then the train curved, and the building disappeared behind the others.

My phone was still warm in my hand.
